equipmentRule: V ≤ 4.5 eyes; V ≤ 7.0 binoculars; otherwise telescope

objects.name: Pleiades
objects.appearance: A knot of six or seven blue stars close together, obvious the moment you notice it.

objects.name: Beehive
objects.appearance: A loose scatter of stars that looks like a smudge until you look slightly away from it.

objects.name: Ptolemy's Cluster
objects.appearance: A big, bright, loose cluster low in the summer south, catalogued by Ptolemy in the second century.

objects.name: Andromeda Galaxy
objects.appearance: The furthest thing the unaided eye can reach: another galaxy, two and a half million light years off.

objects.name: h Persei Cluster
objects.appearance: Two rich clusters side by side in one field, which almost nothing else in the sky does.

objects.name: chi Persei Cluster
objects.appearance: The second half of the Double Cluster, and the richer of the pair in a small telescope.

objects.name: Great Orion Nebula
objects.appearance: A glowing cloud with four young stars at its heart, the nearest place stars are being born.

objects.name: Butterfly Cluster
objects.appearance: A cluster whose brighter stars really do suggest a butterfly's open wings.

objects.name: M22
objects.appearance: One of the closest globular clusters, and one of the few that resolves in binoculars.

objects.name: M35
objects.appearance: A field of a few hundred stars, all much the same brightness, filling a low-power eyepiece.

objects.name: NGC0752
objects.appearance: An open cluster seen as a loose scatter of stars.

objects.name: Lagoon Nebula
objects.appearance: A bright nebula split by a dark lane, with a cluster embedded in it.

objects.name: Hercules Globular Cluster
objects.appearance: A ball of several hundred thousand stars; in a telescope the edges begin to break into points.

objects.name: Eagle Nebula
objects.appearance: The cluster and nebula whose dust pillars are the most reproduced image in astronomy.

objects.name: M15
objects.appearance: A very dense globular with a bright, almost stellar core.

objects.name: Owl Cluster
objects.appearance: A cluster with two bright stars at one end that everyone sees as eyes.

objects.name: M92
objects.appearance: A compact northern globular, often skipped because it stands beside a more famous one.

objects.name: Bode's Galaxy
objects.appearance: A bright spiral galaxy, and one of the few that shows structure in a modest telescope.

objects.name: Saturn Nebula
objects.appearance: A small planetary nebula with faint extensions that suggested a ringed planet.

objects.name: Dumbbell Nebula
objects.appearance: A planetary nebula bright enough to show its shape rather than just its presence.

objects.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
objects.appearance: Two galaxies caught mid-collision, with the spiral arms still traceable.

objects.name: Cat's Eye Nebula
objects.appearance: A bright, compact planetary nebula with a visibly blue-green cast.

objects.name: Sombrero Galaxy
objects.appearance: An edge-on galaxy with a dust lane across a bright bulge, which is where the hat comes from.

objects.name: Crab Nebula
objects.appearance: What is left of a star seen to explode in 1054, and the first object in Messier's list.

objects.name: Cigar Galaxy
objects.appearance: An edge-on galaxy crossed by dust, being torn about by the one beside it.

objects.name: Ring Nebula
objects.appearance: A small, distinct smoke ring — the classic first planetary nebula for a new telescope.
